passage: I'm Nasreen, the third person in the flat, and I was in the kitchen when it turned. Afreen and Jagdish had started on who ate whose leftover biryani. Five minutes later it wasn't about biryani. "You just don't care about anyone but yourself," Afreen said. Jagdish's face went hard. "And you think you're better than all of us because your parents pay your rent." "That's not—" "Don't even. I know what you think." Every time one of them said "that's not true", the other rolled their eyes as if it proved the point. I stood holding a spoon, watching them argue with people who weren't in the room: the Afreen in Jagdish's head, the Jagdish in Afreen's. I couldn't tell who was right. I'm not sure either of them was really listening.

qa.q: What did the argument start about?
qa.a: Afreen and Jagdish had started on who ate whose leftover biryani.

qa.q: What does each of them believe when the other says "that's not true"?
qa.a: Each is frustrated and certain their guess about the other's motives is fact, so the denial only seems like more proof.

qa.q: What could break the mind-reading at this stage?
qa.a: One of them could ask instead of tell, such as "Is that what you think I mean? What did you mean?", and Nasreen could suggest a pause.

qa.q: How is the argument affecting Nasreen?
qa.a: Nasreen feels stuck and helpless in the kitchen, holding a spoon, unable to tell who is right while the two talk past each other.

grounding: Shows two flatmates turning a small quarrel into sweeping claims about each other's motives, hearing every denial as proof.

passage:
Tuesday: Vishal forgot to send his part of the group report. Rajni messaged, "The deadline is Friday, please?"
Wednesday: Still nothing. In the college corridor, Rajni said, "You just don't care about this project, or about any of us." Vishal flushed. "Right, because you think you're smarter than everyone in the group." "I never said that." "You didn't have to." Rajni heard his answer as proof she'd been right about him all along, and her denial sounded to him like one more lie.
Saturday: They met at the canteen to submit it late. Vishal admitted his grandmother had been in hospital all week. Rajni went quiet. She had built a whole story about him, and none of it had been checked.

qa.q: What did Vishal forget to send on Tuesday?
qa.a: He forgot to send his part of the group report.

qa.q: Why did Vishal hear Rajni's "I never said that" as a lie?
qa.a: Feeling stung and already sure she thought herself smarter than everyone, he heard her denial as one more lie instead of new information.

qa.q: What could either of them have done on Wednesday instead of guessing motives?
qa.a: Rajni could have asked "Is something going on?", and Vishal could have shared what was happening instead of answering with an accusation.

qa.q: What might Rajni be feeling on Saturday when she hears about the hospital?
qa.a: She likely feels embarrassed and sorry, seeing that the story she built about him was never checked with him.

grounding: Shows two students assigning motives to each other and treating those guesses as fact, so every denial sounds like a lie.

passage:
Day one: Tejas missed the project meeting at the library. Hrithik texted, "Where are you?" No reply.
Day three: At the canteen, Hrithik didn't ask why. "You just don't care about this project, or about us." Tejas's jaw set. "And you think you're better than everyone because you topped last sem." "That's not true." "Yeah, sure it isn't."
Each denial sounded to the other like one more lie.
Day six: They sat at opposite ends of the lab. Hrithik was sure he knew exactly what Tejas thought of him. Tejas was just as sure. Neither had asked a single question since day one.

qa.q: Where was the project meeting Tejas missed?
qa.a: At the library.

qa.q: What was Hrithik feeling when he said Tejas didn't care?
qa.a: He felt hurt and angry, and he had already decided Tejas's motive, so it came out as a charge rather than a question.

qa.q: What turning point was available at this stage?
qa.a: Either of them could have asked a real question, like why Tejas missed the meeting, instead of assigning motives and treating them as fact.

qa.q: What is Tejas experiencing when he hears "you just don't care"?
qa.a: He feels judged and defensive, which is why he fires back that Hrithik thinks he is better than everyone.

grounding: Over a week, two students move from a missed meeting to accusing each other's motives, and each denial sounds like another lie.

passage:
Ganga, you're twenty now, so I'll tell you what I learnt at your age, in the girls' hostel in Jabalpur.
I'm Neelam Masi, and my roommate then was a quiet girl who kept to herself. One night I said, "You never eat with us. You think you're better than us." She said, "No, I just—" and I said, "Don't lie." And she said, "You all just don't care about anyone outside your group."
After that, anything she said, I heard it as a trick. Anything I said, she heard it as a sneer.
It was months before I found out she was sending her mess money home to her sister.

qa.q: Where was the girls' hostel Neelam Masi lived in?
qa.a: In Jabalpur.

qa.q: What was young Neelam feeling when she accused the roommate?
qa.a: She felt left out and resentful, and was so sure of the roommate's motive that she heard any denial as a lie.

qa.q: In the story, what moment could have changed everything?
qa.a: When the roommate began "No, I just—", young Neelam could have let her finish and asked why she didn't eat with them, instead of saying "Don't lie."

qa.q: What was the roommate going through during those months?
qa.a: She was probably hurt and lonely, judged as proud while she was quietly sending her mess money home to her sister.

grounding: An aunt recalls how, as a student, she and her roommate assigned each other motives and heard every denial as a lie.

passage:
The power had been out in the Panjim flat since six, the rent was due at nine, and Francis's share was short again.
"You just don't care about paying on time," Lokesh said, holding up his phone torch.
"And you think you're better than me because your parents send you money," Francis shot back.
"That's not what I think."
"Don't pretend."
In the torchlight, Lokesh's face looked hard. Francis was sure he could see contempt there. Lokesh was sure Francis was dodging. Every time one said "that's not true," the other heard a lie.
The landlord's knock came at five past nine, and neither of them moved to open the door.

qa.q: What time was the rent due?
qa.a: At nine.

qa.q: What was Francis feeling when he accused Lokesh of thinking he was better?
qa.a: He felt ashamed and defensive about being short on rent, and he was sure he saw contempt in Lokesh's face.

qa.q: What turning point is available here?
qa.a: One of them could stop guessing motives and ask plainly, for example what happened with the rent this month, before the landlord arrives.

qa.q: What is Lokesh experiencing as Francis accuses him?
qa.a: He feels misjudged and frustrated, sure Francis is dodging and that his own denials are not being believed.

grounding: Under time pressure in a dark flat, two young men assign motives to each other and hear every denial as a lie.

passage:
By ten at night in their Andheri flat, Darshan and Harish weren't talking about the electricity bill anymore.

"You just don't care about anything in this flat," Darshan said. "You don't care about me, you don't care about the bills."

"And you think you're better than us because your job pays more," Harish shot back. "Don't pretend you don't."

"I never said that!"

"You didn't have to. It's how you look at my room."

Darshan laughed, a bitter sound. "See, now you're reading my mind. That's convenient."

"Oh, so now I'm lying?"

Darshan had never thought about Harish's room at all. Harish had once, honestly, forgotten the bill by accident. But neither of them could hear the other's denial now. Every "I didn't mean that" sounded like one more lie.

qa.q: Where did Darshan and Harish live?
qa.a: They lived in a flat in Andheri.

qa.q: What was Darshan feeling behind that bitter laugh?
qa.a: Darshan felt frustrated and misjudged, accused of thoughts never actually held, and the anger hardened.

qa.q: What could either of them do to break this pattern?
qa.a: One of them could stop guessing motives and say only what happened and how it felt, or suggest a pause before talking again.

qa.q: How does Harish see Darshan at this point?
qa.a: Harish sees Darshan as looking down on Harish and treats that guess as fact, so any denial sounds false.

grounding: Two flatmates move to 'you just don't care' and 'you think you're better than us', treating guessed motives as fact so denials sound like lies.
